justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons were anchored heavily on the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with only modest drift built in. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of roughly 42.91 reflected near-term momentum and the assumption that absent any major catalyst, prices tend to revert or continue gradually along their recent trend. For the one-week estimate of around 42.97, I incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting mild bullish drift typical of the asset class, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for sentiment shifts to begin mattering. The one-month estimate of 43.18 extended that logic further, essentially projecting a continuation of the gentle upward trend while recognizing that mean-reversion forces and fundamental valuations would begin to assert more influence at that timescale.

The confidence interval widths reflect a deliberate scaling with time horizon, as uncertainty compounds the further out one looks. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly plus or minus 1.27 around the point estimate reflects relatively low realized volatility and the dampening effect of market microstructure over short windows. By one week, the interval widens to nearly plus or minus 2.85, capturing the possibility of macro data releases, central bank communications, or sector-specific news that could shift sentiment meaningfully. The one-month interval of plus or minus nearly 6 points reflects the full range of plausible outcomes when economic conditions, earnings, and geopolitical developments are given room to evolve.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden risk-off episode driven by deteriorating macroeconomic data, a credit event, or escalating geopolitical tension could produce a sharp sell-off that breaks through the lower bound even at the one-week horizon. On the upside, a surprise policy pivot, stronger-than-expected earnings, or a short-covering rally could drive prices beyond the upper bound of my one-month interval. Liquidity conditions also matter: thin markets can amplify moves in either direction, particularly around scheduled events like central bank meetings or major economic releases.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. The assumptions embedded in the forecast — about drift, volatility, and mean reversion — are themselves imprecise, and a structural break in any of those relationships would invalidate the intervals entirely. Investors should treat these figures as probabilistic guidance rather than precise predictions, and should stress-test their positions against scenarios that sit well outside the stated confidence bands.
